slides.title: You’re adding an agent to the support team.
slides.notes:
Set the context before naming the harness. We are building a support agent that can change account state, so a plausible reply is not enough. The company and customer accounts are fictional. The Python operations, model requests, traces, and checks are real workshop code. The one-page handbook is an opening illustration, not the measured starting harness. Participants will build and test the starting version before comparing changes.
Setting frame: point to the active work object, then advance to the complete explanation. This is an illustrated situation, not an execution screenshot. Back restores the scene; the following diagram reveals keep their original order.

slides.title: Acme wants a duplicate $49 charge refunded.
slides.notes: Source: cases.py, double-charge. Its mission explicitly says to keep pay-1 and refund the duplicate. Both pay-1 and pay-2 are captured 4900-cent payments for inv-1, and refunds starts empty. Ask what must be read before changing anything: the account identity, invoice identity, payment identity and existing refunds. Another account also has inv-1, so searching by invoice alone is insufficient. No real payment service is connected.
slides.concept: Acme wants a duplicate $49 charge refunded

slides.title: Check the account after the agent says it has finished.
slides.notes: Read the desired outcome from left to right. The tool appends one full 4900-cent refund for pay-2. Both captured payment records remain; there is no modeled account balance or payment deletion. The independent scorer compares the whole resulting account with the expected account and checks that the requested work was completed. A separate LLM judge compares the employee’s explanation with its recorded actions. A reply saying the refund is complete cannot create a missing refund or excuse a duplicate. These are expected fixture states, not recorded performance results.
slides.concept: Check the account after the agent says it has finished

slides.title: Fern needs Alex added to its account.
slides.notes: Source: cases.py, missing-seat, and simulator.py, provision_timeout_after_commit. Fern starts active and paid, with members empty. The requested email is alex@example.test and the requested role is member. The first provisioning write commits before the injected timeout is returned. From the timeout alone, the agent cannot establish whether access exists; onboarding_status can read the account. The expected final state contains exactly one matching membership, with unrelated state unchanged. This is a separate development case from Acme, not the same account continued into another task. The later MCP and timeout exercises show the implementation and recovery choices.
slides.concept: Fern needs Alex added to its account

slides.title: Our dataset is six tickets with resettable account records.
slides.notes: The dataset is executable teaching fixtures in cases.py, not a collection of historical customer chats. The two development cases let us explain and test the mechanics. The four final cases vary the billing or access situation; their expected outcomes and grader output stay outside improvement prompts. Source files are public, so learners can inspect them, but the final comparison is only informative if we stop choosing edits before running it. Every candidate starts with the same initial account state; one candidate’s refund cannot carry into another candidate’s test. We will first write an instruction change ourselves, then ask an editor agent to propose and test alternatives. The research question in this small workshop is whether those changes affect correct work on fresh tickets. Six cases do not establish production reliability.
slides.concept: Our dataset is six tickets with resettable account records

slides.title: Implement the agent, evaluate it, then test harness changes.
slides.notes: One four-hour session. The schedule includes two ten-minute breaks and hands-on coding. slides.title: A timed-out write may already have worked
slides.notes:
In notebook step 3, use the free local timeout practice. Predict the member count, trigger the timeout, and compare reading status with same-ID and new-ID retries. Reset between alternatives. This uses Python only, changes no saved employee run, and makes no model request. Illustration of simulator.execute after a committed provisioning request. The same operation_id and identical arguments return the stored receipt with replayed=true. A new operation_id is a new mutation and can add a duplicate membership. Reusing an ID with different arguments is rejected. The recorded onboarding recovery read status instead of retrying, so this diagram explains tool behavior rather than claiming this branch occurred in that run.
Visual guide: pending/retry. Advance one state at a time; Back restores the preceding state. The notebook uses the same source figure beside its exercise. Follow the intermediate value to the matching code. These are explanatory frames; they do not execute an experiment or imply a learner result.

slides.title: Four checks answer different questions
slides.notes:
The state scorer reads the account after execution and checks facts such as payment identity, refund amount, and duplicate effects. The LLM judge reads the request, actions, and final reply to assess whether the explanation is supported. These can disagree: an agent may do the right work and describe it incorrectly. An unavailable judge response stays missing.

slides.title: Management would like to automate management.
slides.notes:
The editor uses the same fixed model, but its request is to revise the harness rather than resolve a customer ticket. We supply the current configuration and a saved execution. The permitted edits are instructions, the verification skill, and bounded workflow rules. Tools and scoring stay fixed so any measured difference concerns the harness we changed.
Setting frame: point to the active work object, then advance to the complete explanation. This is an illustrated situation, not an execution screenshot. Back restores the scene; the following diagram reveals keep their original order.
slides.concept: Management would like to automate management

slides.title: Propose two edits to the same starting harness.
slides.notes: Propose asks the editor for two competing changes, such as clearer verification instructions or a mandatory completion check. A and B start from the same parent. Neither receives the other candidate’s test result at this point. We review their saved configurations before allowing the probes.
slides.concept: Propose two edits to the same starting harness

slides.title: Run each candidate from the original account state.
slides.notes: If candidate A has already issued a refund, B must not inherit that refunded account. The controller resets the case before each probe. Compare the actions and returned state of both runs; a successful tool response alone does not tell us the ticket was handled correctly.
slides.concept: Run each candidate from the original account state

slides.title: Test a changed procedure on the same ticket
slides.notes:
Compose receives the proposed configurations and both execution records. It can choose A or B, combine parts of them, or retain the parent. Its rationale explains that choice, but the choice still needs an execution. The solid paths show versions; colors identify alternatives rather than scores.
Visual guide: pending/changes. Advance one state at a time; Back restores the preceding state. The notebook uses the same source figure beside its exercise. Follow the intermediate value to the matching code. These are explanatory frames; they do not execute an experiment or imply a learner result.
slides.concept: Compare the probe results before selecting a harness

slides.title: Execute the harness returned by the composition decision.
slides.notes: A combination may differ from both tested candidates, so we run the returned configuration as its own probe. A Retain decision also runs through this step without inventing a new executable version. We can then inspect the specific execution associated with the decision.
slides.concept: Execute the harness returned by the composition decision

slides.title: Save the selected harness and a lesson for onboarding.
slides.notes: Reflect asks the editor what it learned from the selected run and where that conclusion may not apply. We keep the lesson with that run, then execute the selected harness on onboarding before proposing more changes. This carried-harness teaching protocol differs from the full upstream Harness² cross-task procedure.
slides.concept: Save the selected harness and a lesson for onboarding

slides.title: Require a passing check of the current state before finish.
slides.notes: The loop stores last_check with passed and the digest of world. With verify_before_finish true, finish is rejected if that check is absent, failed, or no longer matches the current state. This is a runtime completion rule. check_work gives public development feedback; the independent final scorer separately checks entire expected accounts and the required resolution.
